items.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime | Microsoft Security Blog
items.excerpt: Microsoft researchers dissect the sprawling phishing infrastructure ecosystem fueling global cybercrime. The report details how threat actors leverage compromised domains, bulletproof hosting, and automated domain generation algorithms to evade takedowns. Infrastructure defenders gain actionable IOCs, architectural breakdowns of phishing-as-a-service platforms, and mitigation strategies for DNS sinkholing and certificate transparency monitoring.

items.title: Inside Wazza: A Newly Observed Device Code Phishing Kit Targeting Microsoft 365 Accounts
items.excerpt: Level Blue analyzes the Wazza phishing kit, a newly observed tool exploiting Microsoft 365 device code authorization flows. The kit bypasses traditional MFA by prompting users to approve sign-ins on secondary devices. The report provides technical breakdowns of the kit’s deployment mechanisms, proxy infrastructure, and detection signatures for SIEM and email security gateways.

items.title: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing | Microsoft Security Blog
items.excerpt: Microsoft Security researchers expose EvilTokens, a sophisticated device code phishing operation targeting enterprise identity providers. The campaign uses custom proxy servers to intercept authorization codes and issue valid OAuth tokens. Defenders receive guidance on monitoring conditional access policies, detecting token theft patterns, and implementing phishing-resistant MFA.

items.title: Abuse of Cloud-Native Infrastructure in Modern Phishing Campaigns - CYFIRMA
items.excerpt: CYFIRMA examines how modern phishing campaigns abuse cloud-native services like serverless functions, object storage, and CDN providers to host malicious payloads and landing pages. The analysis highlights evasion techniques, cost-effective infrastructure scaling, and defensive recommendations for cloud workload protection and traffic anomaly detection.

items.title: Inside an AI‑enabled device code phishing campaign | Microsoft Security Blog
items.excerpt: Microsoft details an AI-driven phishing campaign that dynamically generates realistic login pages and contextual prompts to trick users into authorizing device code sign-ins. The report covers LLM-assisted content generation, infrastructure pivoting, and identity protection controls to block suspicious consent grants and anomalous device approvals.

items.title: Microsoft 365 device code phishing campaign bypasses password stealing | RL Blog
items.excerpt: ReversingLabs investigates a targeted campaign exploiting Microsoft 365 device code flows to circumvent password-based security controls. The report details the attack chain, infrastructure hosting on legitimate cloud platforms, and mitigation strategies including conditional access restrictions, user training, and real-time identity threat monitoring.

items.title: Device Code Phishing is an Evolution in Identity Takeover | Proofpoint US
items.excerpt: Proofpoint explores how device code phishing has matured from a niche tactic to a primary identity takeover vector. The article outlines campaign lifecycles, infrastructure reuse patterns, and behavioral indicators. It provides actionable detection rules for email filters, identity governance platforms, and network telemetry to disrupt credential harvesting pipelines.

items.title: Pro-Russian hackers pose as Ukraine's cyber agency to target government, businesses | The Record from Recorded Future News
items.excerpt: Recorded Future tracks a geopolitical spear-phishing operation where threat actors impersonate Ukraine’s cyber agency to target government and business entities. The campaign leverages tailored lures, compromised credentials, and infrastructure mimicking official domains. Defenders gain insights into attribution indicators, domain reputation analysis, and email authentication hardening.

items.title: CVE-2026-118527
items.excerpt: Use of predictable filenames in Ivanti Connect Secure before versions 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6 allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload files with attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

items.title: CVE-2026-113373

A user whose account was disabled or locked by an administrator in Nexus Repository can sign in again with valid identity provider credentials for the same account, and then receives a new session with the roles of that account.
